title: Meru and the turning Wheel
summary: The Akashic myth of a lost paradise at the centre of the Wheel.

claims.text: Akashic teaching holds that a few fully enlightened beings from an earlier cosmos made a home at the centre of the Wheel.
Shambhala, Golconda and even Avalon are taken as faded memories of Meru, the paradise those sages built.
The cosmos is said to remake itself in human shape, with Pangu and Purusa as names for the divided Cosmic Body.

title: Akashic sects
summary: The many faces of the Brotherhood behind the monk image.

claims.text: The image of bald monks and martial artists hides a large and varied Tradition; outsiders mostly met its warriors and leaders, the Vajrapani and Kannagara.
Many Akashics stayed out of the Western war, finding raids on Technocratic Constructs foolish beside the quiet economic tactics of the Golden Dragons.
With the war for reality now fought mostly in shadow, the other Traditions prize the subtle methods the Brotherhood always used.

title: Shi-Ren
summary: The Benevolent Aristocrats, or Jade Robes.

claims.text: The first Shi-Ren came from Western Chou nobles who lost power in the Warring States era and leaned toward Legalism.
Akashics urged such lords to seek deeper meaning in the laws they enforced, and won a small alliance of nobles weary of endless strife.
Shi-Ren influence faded under the Han and Tang, when the Wu Lung held sway, and many moved to Japan in the 7th century; the Mongol conquest later ruined those left behind.
The sect follows Mo-tzu, a pacifist skilled in war who defended small states and rejected the idea that some lives matter more to Heaven.
At first the Kannagara would not accept Mohists as a sect, until a protest at Omei Shan called the 108 Burning Days won them recognition.
Rivals call them the Mongrel Dharma, a name many Li-Hai take as praise.

title: Kannagara
summary: The Phoenix Robes, keepers of the Elder Path.

claims.text: Kannagara trace their line to Meru, where the first Akasha's sermon is said to have Awakened the Garuda Valley people.
Early contact with forerunners of the Euthanatos began as alliance and turned to conflict in the Himalayan War.
After that war, the Brotherhood began to induct every member into the Kannagara for a time, and Chakravanti later let Kannagara monks follow Buddhism across their lands.

title: Jnani
summary: Hermits, shamans and wandering sages of the Brotherhood.

claims.text: The Jnani are among the three oldest Akashic sects from the Garuda Valley, and their practice changes with each local culture.
In the Himalayan War they used divination and spirit binding against Chakravanti necromancy, and learned much about karma in return.
In Tibet their blend with Bon shamanism set Jnani Bonpo against Kannagara who promoted Buddhism.
Jnani hermitages offered spirit help and charms to common people, which made them targets of Wu Lung and Dalou'laoshi purges.

title: Vajrapani
summary: The Warring Fists of the Brotherhood.

claims.text: When the Wu Lung broke the Shaolin Temple, Vajrapani joined many anti-Qing movements, often with the Shi-Ren.
Against Western imperialism some Warring Fists joined the Shi-Ren in the Golden Dragons, while others went to the Americas or into hiding.
The Second World War and the annexation of Korea split the sect; Chinese and Korean members still shun Japanese Vajrapani.
Today they recruit mainly through traditional martial arts schools with very harsh training.

title: Do, the Way
summary: The secret holistic art of the Akashayana.

claims.text: Do is almost never taught outside the Brotherhood, and outsiders can only guess at it from the many disciplines it shaped.
It springs from Meru's sages, who did every act, from gardening to war, with the same focus and sincerity.
The Vajrapani created Wu Chuan to guard the Jnani and Kannagara, and the Brotherhood taught diluted gate arts to common folk to keep its deadliest methods hidden.

title: The Brotherhood in modern Asia
summary: Pressures on the Akashayana in China, India and Japan.

claims.text: In China the Brotherhood must guard its dragon nests from Kuei-jin and shifters while monasteries are torn down for new building.
In India relations with the Euthanatos have improved, yet only Buddhist and Jain Kannagara ascetics stay there long.
In Japan the Zaibatsu turns dragon lines away from Akashic shrines and the kami have gone quiet.
